newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Heart specialists see Yeltsin for surgery decision.
newsitem.headline: Heart specialists see Yeltsin for surgery decision.

text.p: Heart specialists gathered at a Moscow hospital on Wednesday to assess the condition of Russian President Boris Yeltsin and take a medical decision with huge political consequences.
Leading Russian and foreign doctors discussed a planned heart operation and exactly what needs to be done.
At stake is more than the life of one man, but supreme power in the world's largest country, with a vast nuclear arsenal and still-fragile democratic and market reforms.
Yeltsin, 65, has been in hospital since September 13 and aides say doctors are conducting tests and preparing him for a bypass operation to improve blood supply to the heart.

The Kremlin says the president is in full control of affairs of state, working on documents for up to 2-1/2 hours a day. But Yeltsin's prolonged hospital stay has prompted speculation that his health is poorer than indicated.

The doctors, including pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, entered the Central Clinical Hospital in a convoy of limousines for a scheduled meeting with Yeltsin that is expected to set the date and conditions for heart bypass surgery.
Russian heart specialist Yevgeny Chazov arrived in the first car and DeBakey in another.
Russian officials have said DeBakey, 88, will advise the Russian team but will not take part in the operation itself.
Chief surgeon Renat Akchurin on Tuesday ruled out cancelling the surgery -- a statement that bolstered Russian shares on Wednesday, lifting prices by about one percent in early trade.
It is not clear when the specialists will reveal their recommendations, but some members of the medical team have said it could be several days before a decision is made public.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted hospital officials as saying the doctors' council started at about noon (0800 GMT) but this could not be immediately confirmed.

Akchurin, who is expected to lead the team that will operate on the president, said in a television interview at the weekend that the surgery could be postponed for up to two months to allow Yeltsin to prepare better and gain strength.
Interfax news agency said Akchurin would head to the German city of Hanover to consult with German specialists after the doctors' meeting with Yeltsin.
The liberal newspaper Sevodnya said cancellation or a lengthy postponement of the operation could plunge the country into uncertainty that Yeltsin's opponents were sure to exploit.
"Even if an operation is not necessary on patient Yeltsin, President Yeltsin will have to be operated on," Sevodnya said. "Otherwise, he can expect to face a major scandal."
Yeltsin himself said surgery was necessary if he were to continue to lead an active political life. The operation, which usually involves bypassing damaged arteries with ones from the leg, is common.
The risk of dying is about five percent in Russia, but doctors say it could be greater for Yeltsin if he has serious liver or kidney problems which have not been disclosed.
Russia's communist opposition have already accused Yeltsin of deceiving the electorate in the July 3 election, which gave him another four years in office.

Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and Akchurin said he may have had a third between the first and second rounds of voting. At the time, Yeltsin disappeared from public view but aides insisted that he was merely exhausted and had a cold.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Tuesday Yeltsin's resignation now was out of the question.
Yeltsin has already handed over some powers to Chernomyrdin, his constitutional substitute, and said he would put the prime minister in complete charge while he is being operated on.

The president's absence from the political scene has fuelled speculation about a power struggle between Chernomyrdin and presidential administration chief Anatoly Chubais on the one hand and security supremo Alexander Lebed on the other.
